metadata.title: Discrimination of the Contextual Features of Top Performers in Scientific Literacy Using a Machine Learning Approach

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 student sampling weights provided by OECD to produce unbiased population estimates, and it states that these weights were fully considered in the analysis. The analytic sample is restricted to students who took the computer-based science tests and to countries/economies that used the computer-based assessment mode for the new science components. The paper does not report the specific weight variable name nor any replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so variance estimation details cannot be verified from the text. Because the main modeling is SVM/SVM-RFE with scikit-learn, the manuscript does not clarify whether weights were incorporated into the SVM training procedure or only used for descriptive/thresholding steps; analysts should check the implementation to confirm weight usage in the classifier.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 science scores and questionnaire responses, restricting to (a) students who took the computer-based tests (new science components for this cycle) and (b) countries/economies that used the computer-based assessment mode. For questionnaires, only the student and school principal questionnaires were used because they were required across countries; optional parent/teacher questionnaires were excluded. After cleaning to address missing values, the final analytic dataset contained 380,771 students from 58 countries/economies, including 25,181 top performers at proficiency level 5 or 6. Performance outcome was dichotomized as top performers (level 5–6) vs non-top performers (below level 5).

main_findings.target_variable: Top performer in science literacy (level 5–6 vs below 5)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SVM-RFE feature selection; optimal top-20 feature set. Accuracy (top-20 set): 69.52% ± 4.40% (10-fold CV during feature-set selection). Confirmed performance (two rounds of 10-fold CV): Round 1 average accuracy 77.50% (recall 78.48%); Round 2 average accuracy 75.80% (recall 76.39%).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Science (computer-based) the study leveraged perceived feedback (PERFEED), highest parental education (PARED), disciplinary climate (DISCLISCI), out-of-school study time (OUTHOURS), and science self-efficacy (SCIEEFF) (among an optimal set of 20 contextual features) to predict top performers in science literacy (level 5–6 vs below 5), finding that teacher instructional practices, parents’ educational/occupational status, classroom disciplinary climate, learning time/involvement, school ICT resources, teacher quantity, and students’ self-efficacy were the most predictive. This indicates that strengthening science teaching feedback/adaptation, supporting student self-efficacy, and improving school learning resources and classroom climate may improve the likelihood of reaching top science proficiency, though the results are descriptive/predictive and not causal.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2015 science data from 380,771 secondary students across 58 countries/economies, restricting to students who took the computer-based science tests and using only the required student and school principal questionnaires. The outcome is dichotomized as top performers (scientific literacy proficiency level 5–6) versus non-top performers (below level 5), and the science score is derived from PV1SCIE (first plausible value). The authors apply SVM-RFE to rank 141 contextual variables and select an optimal top-20 feature set, then train an SVM classifier evaluated with 10-fold cross-validation. During feature-set selection, the top-20 set achieved mean accuracy 69.52% (±4.40%); in two follow-up rounds, average accuracy was 77.50% (recall 78.48%) and 75.80% (recall 76.39%). Missing values are imputed using nearest-neighbor approaches (student- and school-level), and the paper states PISA sampling weights were fully considered, but it does not report replicate-weight handling or detailed weight integration in SVM training. Because the model is predictive and based on self-reported contextual variables, the identified features should not be interpreted as causal effects.
